business_problem: Explosive ordnance poses a changing battlefield threat, and bomb-disposal experts need to identify it quickly while reducing their exposure to explosive hazards.
solution_summary: During the several-week trial, sensors onboard small uncrewed aerial systems captured data over varied terrain and land environments, and that data was relayed to Army operators. Operators used AI tools to locate and identify replica mines and explosive ordnance; the trial also showed that AI models could be rapidly retrained for emerging threat types and adapted to different environments. Dstl ran the work on behalf of the British Army with 33 Engineer Regiment (Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Search), linking the sensor-equipped aircraft, threat-recognition tools and bomb-disposal users. The source does not name a model, drone, software product, storage service, or network integration, and does not specify where inference or retraining ran, whether data was persisted, or how results were displayed. It reports faster threat recognition and reduced personnel exposure, but gives no measured performance results.
data_flow: Sensors onboard small uncrewed aerial systems captured data over varied terrain and relayed it to Army operators; operators used AI tools to locate and identify landmines and explosive ordnance. The page does not specify where AI inference ran, how detections were stored, or any further downstream system.
integration_points: Sensors onboard small uncrewed aerial systems
business_outcome: The trial showed that AI-enabled drone technology could help bomb-disposal experts identify threats and conduct missions faster while reducing personnel exposure to explosive hazards. Further trials are planned to mature the technology and inform procurement of a deployable capability.
architecture_clues: Trial conducted at 33 Engineer Regiment's Essex base.
Testing covered varied terrain and land environments.

source_references.title: AI-powered drones to detect explosive threats and protect military personnel

evidence_quotes: Data captured by sensors onboard small uncrewed aerial systems was relayed to Army operators, who used AI tools to locate and identify the munitions.
The trial also successfully demonstrated the ability to rapidly retrain AI models to recognise emerging threat types and adapt to different environments.
The equipment being developed by Dstl will allow EOD operators to conduct their mission faster and will remove people from the explosive hazard.
